findings.title: match_count increment is a read-modify-write race
findings.body: `should_block?` loads the record, computes `record.match_count += 1` in Ruby and then saves. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked address will both read the same `match_count` and write the same value back, so matches are silently lost. Use an atomic update (e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or `increment!`) instead of a full object save.

findings.title: Validation has a DB side effect, so match statistics are double-counted
findings.body: `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which writes to the database (increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`). Validation is not idempotent and is run multiple times per request: `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), each of which runs the email validator, so a single signup attempt bumps `match_count` twice. Any other code that calls `valid?` on a user will also inflate the counters. The statistics gathering should be moved out of the validator (or made explicitly once-per-attempt).

findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case sensitive and not normalized
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` compares the raw value passed in by the validator against the stored string. Email local parts/domains are commonly entered with different casing (e.g. `Block@SpamFromHome.org`), and the `users.email` column is not guaranteed to be downcased at validation time, so a blocked address can be bypassed just by changing capitalization. Normalize (downcase/strip) both on write and on lookup, or compare with `lower(email)`.

findings.title: Failed save of match statistics is silently swallowed
findings.body: `record.save` is used without checking the return value. Because the model also runs presence/uniqueness validations on save, a failure (or a validation error introduced later) silently discards the `match_count`/`last_match_at` update with no log, making the statistics quietly unreliable.

findings.title: Mutable array declared on the controller class is shared between instances
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` puts a single array on the class prototype; `pushObject` in `createAccount` mutates that shared array. Any second instance of `CreateAccountController` (or the same instance reused across modal open/close) sees another instance's rejected emails, and the state is never reset. Initialize it per instance (e.g. in `init`) instead of as a class-level literal.

findings.title: Server-side email error reason is replaced by generic "invalid" message
findings.body: When the server rejects an email (blocked address, domain not allowed, already taken, …) the controller pushes the value into `rejectedEmails` and the validation then shows `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. The specific reason returned in `result.errors.email` (including the new `user.email.blocked` string added to server.en.yml) is discarded, so users get a misleading "Email is invalid" message for an address that is syntactically valid. Use the server-supplied error text keyed by email instead of a generic constant.

findings.title: No coverage for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator
findings.body: The `email_domains_whitelist` / `email_domains_blacklist` behaviour was removed from `User#email_validator` and re-implemented here (including the `elsif` precedence and the `errors[attribute].blank?` short-circuit that skips the blocked-email check). The new spec only exercises the blocked-email branch, so the relocated domain restriction code and the interaction between the two branches are untested after the refactor.
